questions.question: An aircraft climbs steadily at the climb angle γ, with the thrust close to the flight path. Which balance of forces along the path is right?
options: T = D + mg sin γ: the thrust carries the drag and part of the weight
T = D + mg cos γ: the thrust carries the drag and part of the weight
T = D: the lift carries all of the weight, as in level flight
T = D − mg sin γ: the weight helps the thrust along the path
questions.explanation: The weight points straight down, so its part along the path is mg sin γ, pointing backward. The thrust must carry it on top of the drag. The cosine form gives T = D + mg in level flight, which is wrong; T = D leaves out the weight along the path; the minus sign describes a descent.

questions.question: An aircraft climbs at V = 66 m/s along a path 4° above the horizontal. What is its rate of climb?
questions.explanation: The rate of climb is the vertical part of the speed: R/C = 66 × sin 4° = 66 × 0.0698 = 4.60 m/s. 264 m/s multiplies V by the angle in degrees: the small-angle form Vγ needs γ in radians. 65.8 m/s is V cos γ, the speed over the ground. 0.0698 is sin γ alone, which has no units.

questions.section: Thrust and power required in a climb
questions.question: At the same weight and altitude, how does the curve of thrust required against speed change when the aircraft climbs at a fixed angle γ instead of flying level?
options: It moves up by mg sin γ at every speed
It moves up by mg cos γ at every speed
It rises in proportion to V, mostly at high speed
It stays the same, since lift still balances weight
questions.explanation: In the shallow-climb model the drag at each speed is the drag of level flight, and the climb adds the constant term mg sin γ (or mgγ). The term that grows with V is in the power required, mgγV, not in the thrust. The cosine part of the weight is carried by the lift.

questions.question: An aircraft of weight mg = 80,000 N flies at a speed where PA = 1,600 kW and PR = 700 kW. What is its rate of climb?
questions.explanation: The excess power is 1,600 − 700 = 900 kW = 900,000 W, and R/C = 900,000/80,000 = 11.25 m/s. 0.01125 m/s leaves the power in kW, so it is 1,000 times too small. 20.0 m/s uses the power available alone, and 28.75 m/s adds the two powers. The power required is spent on the drag, so it is subtracted.

questions.question: A jet has a thrust available that does not change with speed. At what speed does it climb most steeply?
options: At the minimum-thrust speed, below its fastest-climb speed
At the minimum-power speed, where the excess power is largest
At its fastest-climb speed, since angle and rate peak together
At its maximum speed, where the engines give the most power
questions.explanation: With a flat thrust available, the excess thrust TA − D is largest where the drag is smallest, at the minimum-thrust speed. The rate of climb multiplies the excess thrust by V, so it peaks at a higher speed. At the maximum speed the excess thrust is zero, and so is the climb.

questions.question: On a plot of rate of climb against horizontal speed, one point for each airspeed, where is the steepest climb?
options: Where a line from the origin just touches the curve
At the top of the curve, where the rate of climb is largest
Where the curve crosses zero, at the highest speed
At the left end of the curve, at the stall speed
questions.explanation: A line from the origin to a point has the slope (V sin γ)/(V cos γ) = tan γ, so the steepest line that still reaches the curve, the tangent, marks the steepest climb. The top of the curve is the fastest climb; where the curve crosses zero the aircraft cannot climb at all.

questions.question: A jet has n T0 = 44,000 N at sea level, a minimum thrust required of 11,000 N and a lapse exponent mad = 0.7. What is ρc/ρ0 at its absolute ceiling?
questions.explanation: At the ceiling n T0 (ρc/ρ0)0.7 = 11,000 N, so (ρc/ρ0)0.7 = 0.25 and ρc/ρ0 = 0.251/0.7 = 0.1380. 0.3789 raises 0.25 to the power 0.7, which applies the lapse the wrong way. 0.25 leaves out the exponent, which is right only when mad = 1. 0.75 is one minus the thrust ratio, which no step of the method uses.

questions.section: One engine out and an obstacle
questions.question: An engine fails just after a climb begins, and a ridge stands ahead. Which speed gives the most height when the aircraft reaches the ridge?
options: The steepest-climb speed, which gains the most height per meter of ground
The fastest-climb speed, which gains the most height per second
The highest speed the engines allow, to reach the ridge sooner
Any speed, because the climb angle is the same at every speed
questions.explanation: Clearing an obstacle depends on the height gained over the distance to it, which is the climb angle. Flying faster can raise the rate of climb, but the aircraft covers the ground even faster and arrives lower. The climb angle changes with speed and peaks at the steepest-climb speed.
